The HTM General Ledger: Supplies, Payroll, Parts, Consumables, Contracts, Training

Unit 1: Financial Management. Lesson 2 of 60 in CHTM Academy.

A cost accountant emails you a spreadsheet of your department's spending and asks you to explain three lines. The lines are not named "parts" and "training". They are six-digit account numbers with abbreviations you have never used. This is the general ledger, and until you can read it you cannot defend a single number in your budget.

What the general ledger is

The general ledger is the hospital's complete record of financial transactions, organized by account. The list of those accounts is the chart of accounts, and it is the hospital's list, not yours. Your budget is reviewed, reported, and questioned in those account numbers. If you track spending in categories you invented, every conversation with finance starts with a translation argument you will lose.

The accounts an HTM department manages

What you spend on                        Where it posts
technician and supervisor wages          salaries and wages
benefits                                 employee benefits, usually a rate on salary
overtime and on-call pay                 salaries, tracked as its own line
repair parts bought by HTM               maintenance and repairs
service contracts and vendor labor       purchased maintenance and repair
shop consumables and small supplies      office supplies or medical and surgical
                                         inventory, by what the item is
test equipment calibration               maintenance and repairs, or a calibration
                                         line where the hospital keeps one
training tuition, travel, lodging        travel and education
software licenses and support            purchased services or software maintenance
a replacement monitoring system          capital, not operating

Training is an expense rather than capital, because knowledge cannot be depreciated. A system purchase is capital and reaches your operating budget only later, as depreciation and as the service that follows it.

Coding a purchase to the right account

Coding is the act of deciding which account number and which cost center a purchase posts to, and it happens when the requisition is written, not at year end. Two habits keep it honest: the account comes from the chart of accounts, and the cost center comes from the asset record of the device the money was spent on.

Encumbrances and accruals in plain words

An encumbrance is money set aside the moment you commit to spend it. The purchase order is raised, the funds are reserved against your budget, and the balance available to you drops even though no invoice has arrived. An accrual records an expense in the month the work or the delivery happened rather than the month the payment cleared. Hospitals budget on an accrual basis, so a part received in June is June's expense even if the invoice is paid in August. Both exist so that your available balance and your reported spending tell the truth about commitments you have already made.

Why miscoded parts hide the real cost of a device

Post a pump part to a generic supplies account and three reports go wrong at once. The device's own cost history understates what it really costs to keep, so the replacement decision is made on a false number. The clinical cost center is never charged, so nursing believes its equipment is free. And the cost of service ratio for that model cannot be calculated at all, which removes the one number that would have proved a contract was overpriced. Reading the ledger detail line by line each month, with the work orders beside it, is how a manager catches that before it becomes a year of bad data.

Exam tip: budget and report in the hospital's account numbers. Parts and in-house repair post to maintenance and repairs; contracts and vendor labor post to purchased maintenance; training posts to travel and education and is never capital. An encumbrance reserves committed money; an accrual books the expense in the month it was incurred.
Remember
The general ledger is the hospital's account structure, and a manager who codes every part, contract, and class to the right account and cost center keeps the cost history that later justifies a replacement.
Deeper explanation

The HTM General Ledger: Supplies, Payroll, Parts, Consumables, Contracts, Training, explained slowly

Reading a ledger detail line

Finance sends you a ledger extract. It looks like this, and every column matters.

Date    Account  Cost ctr  Document   Vendor/Ref         Amount   Note
03-04   6421     7310      PO 84112   Parts supplier      1,284   pump board
03-07   6421     7310      PO 84119   Parts supplier        96    freight only
03-11   6190     7310      JE 2291    payroll             51,604   period 6
03-14   6540     7310      INV 55210  imaging vendor      15,000   contract, qtr 2
03-18   6421     6120      PO 84140   Parts supplier        612    pump board
03-22   6421     7310      PO 84151   Parts supplier         48    fuse, one each

Four things are visible to a manager who knows what to look for. The 03-07 line is freight posted separately from the part, so the device's true parts cost is split across two documents. The 03-18 line posted to a different cost center, 6120, which is either a correct chargeback to a clinical department or a coding error, and only the work order tells you which. The 03-14 contract payment is a quarter of an annual contract, so annualizing a single month's purchased-maintenance figure would overstate the year by four times. And the 03-22 line is a $48 part on its own purchase order, which cost the hospital roughly $100 of overhead to raise: the order cost more than the part.

Encumbrance, accrual, and the balance you can actually spend

Event                                 Budget   Encumbered  Actual   Available
Start of month                        20,000            0        0     20,000
Purchase order raised for a $6,000    20,000        6,000        0     14,000
assembly
Assembly received in the month        20,000            0    6,000     14,000
(accrued as this month's expense)
Invoice paid two months later         20,000            0    6,000     14,000

The available balance drops when you commit, not when you pay. That is the whole point of an encumbrance: it stops two managers from spending the same dollar. The accrual then books the expense in the month the assembly arrived, so the month's report reflects what the department consumed rather than what the payables clerk processed.

The cost of miscoding, demonstrated

Take one imaging system over three years. The true picture and the miscoded picture are both internally consistent, which is why nobody notices.

                              True       As coded      Why
Parts posted to the asset     42,000       11,000      31,000 went to a generic
                                                       supplies account
Vendor labor                  18,000       18,000      posted correctly
Annual service cost            20,000        9,667      three-year average
Original cost               400,000      400,000
Cost of service ratio           5.0%         2.4%       20,000 / 400,000 x 100
                                                       against 9,667 / 400,000

A manager reading the miscoded column sees a cheap, reliable system and leaves the contract alone. A manager reading the true column sees a ratio twice as high and goes looking for the cause. The data did not lie; the coding did.

What to memorize

General ledger      the hospital's record of transactions, organized by account
Chart of accounts   the hospital's list of accounts and cost centers
Parts and in-house  maintenance and repairs
repair
Contracts and       purchased maintenance and repair
vendor labor
Training            travel and education; an expense, never capital
Encumbrance         money reserved the moment it is committed
Accrual             the expense booked in the month it was incurred
Purchase order      roughly $100 of hospital overhead per order
